zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

headline: Solid B+ Week: Spencer Yellowfin Steady, Norfolk Wahoo Crash the Spread
subhead: Warm water pinned against the canyon edges kept the trolling bite honest all week, with Norfolk's wahoo run stealing the show.
body_markdown:
If I'm grading this week, I'm giving it a solid B+. Not the A we had back in mid-July when everything from Spencer to Norfolk was stacked with yellowfin, but a week where every boat I talked to at the Cape May Canyon dock had fish in the box and a story about the one that got off. The knock is consistency — some days you had to run the whole 60 miles to find the right water, other days it was right there waiting on the edge.

Here's the why. The Bight's holding warm, clean water — 75.7°F out at the edge buoy, seas a manageable 3 feet at a long 7-second period, which means it's rollable but fishable, no white-knuckle rides. That warm push has been leaning into the canyon walls at Spencer and Lindenkohl for about ten days now, and it's dragging bait with it. When that happens, the yellowfin quit roaming and start setting up shop on the humps and the 100-fathom curve, which is exactly where we found them.

Spencer's been my go-to this week. Working the north wall around the 100 to 250-fathom transition, trolling a mixed spread — green machines and cedar plugs down the middle, ballyhoo and mullet chains off the riggers — put yellowfin in the 30 to 55-pound range in the box most mornings. Best window was that first hour of light before the wind filled in, water color running that deep cobalt blue right where it meets the green edge. A few boats switched to chunking butterfish once the sun got high and the trolling bite went quiet — that's the move if you're patient, anchor up on the temp break, let the slick build, and wait for that first tuna to show color under the transom.

Lindenkohl was more of a mixed bag. Good bluefin mixed in with the yellowfin trolling the same 100-fathom stretch, but you had to grind for it some afternoons — long stretches of nothing, then a triple hookup out of nowhere. That's canyon fishing in August, though. The fish are there, they're just not dumb about showing themselves in the heat of the day.

Norfolk is where the week got interesting. Wahoo showed up hard on the high-speed gear — planers and wire line pulling Ilanders and cedar plugs at 12 to 15 knots along the drop, and guys were connecting on fish in the 40 to 60-pound class working the edge where Norfolk's wall falls off fast into deep water. That warm water influence Hooper — sorry, that warm water everybody's been talking about — is exactly the kind of setup that pulls wahoo up onto these canyon edges, and Norfolk sits far enough south that it gets the benefit first. If you're chasing wahoo specifically, that's your canyon right now, not Spencer, not Lindenkohl.

Poor Man's stayed quieter, which tracks — it's the shallowest and closest-in of the four, and without a strong bait push it doesn't hold fish the way the deeper canyons do. A couple of mahi came off weed lines drifting rigged ballyhoo and small chunks of butterfish under the color changes, but nobody I talked to made a special trip out there this week. I'd keep it in the back pocket for a quick run if the wind's up and you can't make the longer haul.

Bigeye have been showing at night on the chunk, mostly reported out of Spencer and Lindenkohl both — that's your classic pattern, sun goes down, the bigeye come up off the bottom structure to feed, and a well-soaked chunk bait on circle hooks, lightly weighted, fished way back in the slick will get bit. White marlin have been scattered through all four canyons but nothing consistent enough to call a run yet — a few pulled ballyhoo skirted with blue/white or pink/white got looks, one or two hookups, but I wouldn't build a trip around it just yet.

We flagged this last week — said the softer tides heading toward the coming neap would shift the emphasis toward trolling and the daytime deep-drop, and that's exactly what's playing out. The tide range is narrowing into that August 5-6 neap, current's going slack in the canyon breaks, and that softer water is favoring the troll over the drift-chunk in a lot of spots. If you're rigging for swords, this is the window — daytime deep-drop tactics work better when you're not fighting a hard current to keep your bait down near bottom structure.

Looking ahead, the high pressure's holding, seas stay manageable, and that warm water isn't going anywhere fast. I'd lean Spencer and Lindenkohl for yellowfin and bigeye, and if wahoo's the target, make the longer run to Norfolk while that warm edge is sitting right on the wall. Poor Man's is your backup plan, not your primary. Watch the tide easing into the neap — that's your cue to lean harder on the troll and less on the anchor-up chunk for the next several days.
